questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If ‘x’, ‘v’ and ‘a’ denote the displacement, velocity and acceleration of a particle respectively executing SHM of periodic time t, then which one of the following does not change with time?
questions.solution:
Key Idea for checking the correctness of an equation dimensional analysis is done using the principle of homogeneity.
The dimensions of given variables of SHM are as
Displacement, $\left[x\right] = \left[{M}^{0}L{T}^{0}\right]$
Velocity, $\left[v\right] = \left[{M}^{0}L{T}^{- 1}\right]$
Acceleration, $\left[a\right] = \left[{M}^{0}L{T}^{- 2}\right]$
and time period, $\left[T\right] = \left[{M}^{0}{L}^{0}T\right]$
Now, checking each option for these values for option (a)
$\dfrac{\left[a\right]\left[T\right]}{\left[x\right]} = \dfrac{\left[{M}^{0}L{T}^{- 2}\right]}{\left[{M}^{0}L{T}^{0}\right]} = \left[{M}^{0}{L}^{0}{T}^{- 1}\right]$
As it depends on time, so change with it.
For option (b),
$\left[a\right]\left[T\right] + 2\pi\left[v\right] = \left[{M}^{0}L{T}^{- 2}\right]\left[{M}^{0}{L}^{0}T\right] + \left[{M}^{0}{L}^{0}{T}^{- 1}\right]$
= $\left[{M}^{0}L{T}^{- 1}\right]$
It is also dependent on time and hence changes with it.
For option $\left(c\right)$ ,
$\dfrac{\left[a\right]\left[T\right]}{\left[v\right]} = \dfrac{\left[{M}^{0}L{T}^{- 2}\right]\left[{M}^{0}{L}^{0}T\right]}{\left[{M}^{0}L{T}^{- 1}\right]} = \left[{M}^{0}{L}^{0}{T}^{0}\right]$
As it is a constant having no dimension, so it does not change with time.
For option (d),
$\left[a\right]\left[t\right] + 4{\pi}^{2}{\left[d\right]}^{2} = \left[{M}^{0}L{T}^{- 2}\right]\left[{M}^{0}{L}^{0}T\right] + {\left[{M}^{0}L{T}^{- 1}\right]}^{2}$
$= \left[L{T}^{- 1}\right] + \left[{L}^{2}{T}^{- 2}\right]$
As, the terms is dependent on time, so changes with it.
Also, it is dimensionally incorrect.
Hence, option $\left(c\right)$ is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The SI unit an dimension of Stefan’s constants $\sigma$ in case of Stefan’s law of radiation is
questions.solution:
According to Stefan’s law, energy emitted by a body per unit area per second is proportional to fourth power of the absolute temperature.
$E = \sigmaT^{4}$
where, E = energy emitted/areas/second,
T = absolute temperature in kelvin
And $\sigma$ = Stefan’s constant $⇒ \sigma = \dfrac{E}{T^{4}}$
Unit of Stefan’s constant
$⇒ \dfrac{\dfrac{J}{m^{2}s}}{K^{4}} = \dfrac{J}{m^{2}sK^{4}}$
Dimensions of Stefan’s constant,
$\sigma\dfrac{\left[Energy\right]}{\left[Area\right] \times \left[Time\right] \times {\left[Temperature\right]}^{4}}$
$= \dfrac{ \left[ML^{2}T^{- 2}\right]}{ \left[L^{2}T \timesK^{4}\right]} = \left[M^{1}L^{0}T^{- 3}K^{- 4}\right]$

Electric field, $E = \dfrac{F}{q}$
Where, F = force and q = electric charge
Dimension of E or $\left[E\right] =\dfrac{ \left[MLT^{- 2}\right]}{\left[AT\right]} = \left[MLT^{- 3}A^{- 1}\right]
Power of mass = 1
Electric moment, $m = l \timesA$
where, $l= current and $A = area
Dimension of m = [M] = \left[M^{0}L^{2}T^{0}A\right]
Hence, power of mass =0$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In damped SHM, the SI unit of damping constant is
questions.solution:
In damped SHM, damping force is proportional to the velocity of the oscillator.
$∴$ Damping constant, $b = \dfrac{{F}_{d}}{v}$
SI unit of damping constant
$b = \dfrac{SIunitoffoce}{SIunitofvelocity} = \dfrac{kg. m. s^{2}}{m. s^{- 1}}$
$= kg. s^{- 1} = \dfrac{kg}{s}$
Hence, the SI unit of damping constant is kg/s.
